title: First Female and 24th Chief Justice'
primary_topics: Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro as 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' (Supreme Court Public Information Office source)
De Castro's 42-day tenure (Aug 28 - Oct 9, 2018) -- shortest in history but with 45 years prior government service
Comparison with CJ Pedro L. Yap (72-day tenure, 1988) and CJ Carolina Griño-Aquino-era contexts
De Castro's signature judicial output: Estrada plunder conviction (Sandiganbayan, 2007); Risos-Vidal v. Comelec (2015)
De Castro's Supreme Court vote pattern on major cases (Hacienda Luisita, Truth Commission, PDAF/DAP, Marcos burial, De Lima arrest, Mindanao martial law, Sereno quo warranto)

sub_topics: Source of the 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' title: 'Benchmark,' SC Public Information Office magazine, Vol. 3, No. 4, Special Issue
De Castro began tenure Aug 28, 2018; ended Oct 9, 2018 midnight; mandatory retirement at age 70
10+ years as Associate Justice (Dec 4, 2007 - Aug 27, 2018) before becoming CJ
Comparison: CJ Pedro L. Yap's 72-day tenure (Apr 19 - Jun 30, 1988) and only 2 years as Associate Justice
Distinction: first CJ also to have served as Sandiganbayan presiding justice

Sept 12, 2007 -- De Castro penned 211-page SBN decision convicting Joseph Estrada of plunder (reclusion perpetua, forfeiting >₱549M 'Muslim Youth Foundation' deposit, ₱180M 'Jose Velarde' deposit, the 'Boracay Mansion' in New Manila Quezon City, perpetual disqualification)

Jan 21, 2015 -- De Castro authored Risos-Vidal v. Comelec lifting Estrada's perpetual disqualification on the ground that Arroyo's pardon restored his civil and political rights, allowing him to run and win as mayor of Manila

De Castro's SC vote profile: (1) distributing Hacienda Luisita to farmers; (2) striking down Aquino's Truth Commission; (3) striking down PDAF / DAP; (4) Marcos burial in Libingan ng mga Bayani; (5) upholding De Lima's arrest and detention; (6) upholding Mindanao martial law and its extension; (7) ousting CJ Sereno via quo warranto

Retirement entitlements: emoluments equivalent to incumbent CJ for life (lump sum first 5 years; monthly from year 6); spouse survivorship benefits; 1 month salary/allowances per year of service; monetization of accrued leaves
Retirement honors: SC Session Hall resolution by Associate Justices; sit-down dinner at 5-star hotel
Sereno: served ~6 years as CJ but was ousted via quo warranto, declared 'ineligible' though recognized as 'de facto officer'; no retirement benefits/honors
Corona: served 2 years (May 17, 2010 - May 29, 2012) until Senate impeachment ousted him; no retirement benefits/honors

stances.claim: The honor of being 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' belongs to Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro per the Supreme Court's own Public Information Office magazine 'Benchmark' -- even though her CJ tenure of 42 days (Aug 28 - Oct 9, 2018) was the shortest in history, the longevity of her tenure does not negate the constitutional and titular reality of her holding the office.
stances.rhetorical_move: appeal to authoritative institutional source ('Benchmark') to settle a reader query

stances.claim: De Castro's 42-day CJ tenure rests atop a substantial Supreme Court record spanning Dec 4, 2007 to Aug 27, 2018 -- including her authorship of the 211-page Sandiganbayan plunder conviction of Joseph Estrada (Sept 12, 2007) and her later Supreme Court decision in Risos-Vidal v. Comelec (Jan 21, 2015) lifting Estrada's perpetual disqualification on the basis of Arroyo's pardon -- meaning her judicial significance far exceeds her CJ-tenure days.
stances.rhetorical_move: tenure-vs-record juxtaposition to defend the substantive weight behind a brief titular appointment

stances.claim: De Castro's vote profile on the Supreme Court -- for Hacienda Luisita distribution, against the Truth Commission, against PDAF and DAP, for Marcos burial in Libingan ng mga Bayani, for upholding De Lima's arrest, for Mindanao martial law's constitutionality and extension, and for the quo warranto ouster of Sereno -- places her on the conservative-statist side of many high-stakes constitutional questions of the 2010s.
stances.rhetorical_move: voting-profile catalogue letting the seven items speak for themselves without overt evaluation

stances.claim: Retirement benefits and honors for a CJ are not denied by brevity of tenure but by manner of departure: De Castro retired by reaching 70 and so received full CJ-equivalent emoluments for life plus survivorship benefits, leave monetization, and Session Hall honors; Sereno (ousted by quo warranto, 'declared ineligible' though recognized as a 'de facto officer') and Corona (ousted by Senate impeachment) received none of these because neither retired.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal distinction between retirement-by-age and removal-by-process to explain divergent post-tenure entitlements

notable_anecdotes: The 'Benchmark' source identification -- CJ literally cites the front page of the Supreme Court Public Information Office magazine, Vol. 3 No. 4 Special Issue, to settle reader queries about who is 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' -- a tiny but characteristic show of institutional-source discipline.

The 211-page Sandiganbayan decision convicting Joseph Estrada of plunder (Sept 12, 2007), penned by then-presiding justice De Castro, sentencing him to reclusion perpetua, forfeiting over ₱549 million deposited in the name of the Muslim Youth Foundation, ₱180 million deposited under 'Jose Velarde,' and the 'Boracay Mansion' in New Manila, Quezon City, plus perpetual disqualification -- only for her, eight years later as an SC associate justice, to effectively modify her own ruling via Risos-Vidal v. Comelec.

The doctrinal closing tension -- 'someone who had held it in fact for six years (and expectedly for a record-breaking total of 18 years), and just as suddenly bestow it in law on someone else who by her own declaration never expected it even just for an equally record-breaking 42 days' -- a chiastic doublet that lets CJ underline the strangeness of the title transfer without naming Sereno aggressively.

The retirement-benefits inventory: lump-sum first five years; monthly emoluments for life thereafter; spouse survivorship if she predeceases her husband; one month salary and allowances per year of service; monetization of accrued vacation and sick leaves; a Session Hall resolution; a sit-down dinner for friends and relatives at a 5-star hotel -- making concrete the institutional gulf between retirement and removal.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers readers querying where the title 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' for Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro originated: from the front page of 'Benchmark,' the Supreme Court Public Information Office magazine, Vol. 3 No. 4 Special Issue. He documents De Castro's 42-day CJ tenure (Aug 28 - Oct 9, 2018 midnight) as the shortest in history -- a few days shorter than CJ Pedro L. Yap's 72-day tenure in 1988 -- but anchored in 45 years of government service and 10+ years as an SC Associate Justice (Dec 4, 2007 - Aug 27, 2018), five times Yap's two-year associate stint. She is the only CJ also to have served as Sandiganbayan presiding justice, where she penned the 211-page Sept 12, 2007 decision convicting Joseph Estrada of plunder, sentencing him to reclusion perpetua, forfeiting more than ₱549 million in the Muslim Youth Foundation deposit, ₱180 million in the 'Jose Velarde' deposit, and the 'Boracay Mansion' in New Manila, plus perpetual disqualification -- only for her later, as an SC associate justice, to effectively modify that ruling through Risos-Vidal v. Comelec (Jan 21, 2015), holding that Arroyo's pardon restored Estrada's civil and political rights and allowing him to run and win as Manila mayor. He catalogues her SC vote profile: for distributing Hacienda Luisita to farmers; against Aquino's Truth Commission; against PDAF/DAP; for Marcos's Libingan ng mga Bayani burial; for upholding De Lima's arrest and detention; for the Mindanao martial law and its extension; and for the quo warranto ouster of Sereno. Because she retired by reaching age 70 rather than being removed, De Castro received the full CJ-equivalent retirement entitlement: emoluments for life (lump-sum first five years, monthly thereafter), survivorship benefits for her husband, one month salary and allowances per year of service, leave monetization, and ceremonial Session Hall honors plus a sit-down dinner at a five-star hotel. By contrast, Sereno (ousted by quo warranto, declared ineligible though recognized as a 'de facto officer') and Corona (ousted by Senate impeachment May 29, 2012) received none of these because neither retired -- a doctrinal consequence that CJ closes by noting transferred the title 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' in law to someone who never expected it even for 42 days, away from someone who had held it in fact for six years and expectedly for a record-breaking 18.
